title: The One With The Cuffs

jokes.text: Joey enthusiastically announces free stuff from Treeger; Chandler's deadpan reaction: 'Oh, no. I'm paddling away.'
jokes.setup: Joey excitedly declares they're 'so in luck' and to 'wait right there' as he reveals free stuff from the building super.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately announces he's 'paddling away' — rejecting the premise before even seeing it.
jokes.explanation: A clean Chandler moment — his world-weary deflation of Joey's enthusiasm is perfectly in character. 'Paddling away' is an unusual, slightly absurd word choice that elevates it above a generic putdown. Good economy, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Treeger's giving away free stuff!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not taking it. I don't care if he's giving away a lifetime supply of free stuff, I'm not taking it. That's how it starts, and then before you know it, you're stuck in a canoe with a guy who smells like old cheese.

jokes.text: 'Really? We got all this rusty crap for free?'
jokes.setup: Joey frames the free items from Treeger as a windfall ('we are so in luck').
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry summary — 'rusty crap' — deflates Joey's excitement while being technically accurate.
jokes.explanation: Functional Chandler deadpan. Works as a button on the opening bit, though it doesn't add much beyond the prior joke's premise.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, 'cool stuff' is just a nice way of saying 'junk we don't need'.

jokes.text: 'This and a bunch of bubble wrap. And some of it is not even popped.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just labeled all this free stuff 'rusty crap'.
jokes.punchline: Joey's earnest counter-selling point is unpopped bubble wrap — delivered as if it's genuinely valuable, revealing his low bar for excitement.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Joey joke because it's totally sincere. Unpopped bubble wrap is a genuinely appealing thing, but Joey framing it as a treasure is perfectly character-specific. The 'not even popped' qualifier does a lot of work — it's the kind of detail only Joey would think to mention and only Joey would find persuasive.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I got unpopped bubble wrap!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life!

jokes.text: 'Could we be more white trash?'
jokes.setup: The two are standing surrounded by rusty free junk and bubble wrap.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's rhetorical question names what the audience is already thinking, in his signature 'Could this BE...' construction.
jokes.explanation: This is a signature Chandler catchphrase construction ('Could we BE more...') applied to a relatable situation. The studio audience will respond well. High quotability because it uses his recurring rhetorical device, though the underlying observation isn't particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look at us. We're like a bunch of raccoons going through garbage, except the garbage is free and we're pretending it's treasure.

jokes.text: Monica playing solitaire, talking to herself: 'How desperate am I? Good thing Chandler's not here. He always wins at this game.'
jokes.setup: Monica is playing solitaire alone, muttering to herself about how desperate she is.
jokes.punchline: She's so bored and lonely that she's relieved Chandler isn't around to beat her at solitaire — a game played alone.
jokes.explanation: This is a quietly brilliant absurdist joke. Solitaire is by definition a one-player game, so the idea that Chandler 'always wins' at it is genuinely surreal. It rewards the audience for catching the absurdity while also characterizing Monica's competitive nature perfectly. Strong originality — this isn't a joke you see often.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know I'm desperate, but I'm not Chandler desperate.

jokes.text: 'It'd be a great way to get rid of that last smidgen of self-respect.'
jokes.setup: Monica announces she told her mom she'd cater her mom's party because she needs money.
jokes.punchline: Chandler frames catering for her own mother as the final nail in Monica's dignity coffin.
jokes.explanation: The word 'smidgen' does a lot of heavy lifting here — it implies there's barely any self-respect left to lose, which is funny. Standard Chandler quip but well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I figured if I'm going to destroy my remaining self-respect, I might as well get paid for it.

jokes.text: 'You don't have to stick up for her. She can't hear you.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to defend their mother's decision to hire Monica, saying she wouldn't have done it if Monica weren't good.
jokes.punchline: Monica points out he's sticking up for their mom even though she isn't present — implying he does it reflexively and that Monica doesn't believe it's sincere.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical line that says a lot about the Ross-Monica-Judy dynamic with minimal words. The implication that Ross defends their mother so habitually he does it even when unnecessary is a nice character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, my mother hired who she wanted to hire.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She doesn't need diplomacy, she needs a nap.

jokes.text: 'Do you have any juice?' / 'Just pickle.'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks for juice in what appears to be a normal domestic exchange.
jokes.punchline: Joey has only pickle juice — which he offers without embarrassment as a reasonable alternative.
jokes.explanation: Three words — 'Just pickle' — do all the work. The economy is exceptional. The joke relies entirely on the absurdity of Joey having only pickle juice in his fridge and treating it as a normal thing. Perfect Joey character moment with almost no words wasted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Chandler, you got any juice?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure. I've got pickle juice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pickle juice? Why do you have pickle juice?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I like to drink it straight from the jar. It's refreshing.

jokes.text: Chandler's panicked reaction: 'You didn't say yes to that, did you?' — followed by Joanna walking in the door at [02:18].
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Rachel whether she said yes to Joanna (her boss) offering her a drink. His alarm implies the obvious answer is 'no'.
jokes.punchline: Joanna walks through the door, answering the question visually before any words are spoken.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured piece of visual comedy. The alarm in Chandler's voice sets up the audience's expectation, and Joanna's entrance at exactly the right moment delivers a wordless punchline. The structure is clean and the timing (inferred) is strong. Rewatch bonus because you see it coming on rewatch and still enjoy the execution.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You said you'd never get married.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know what I said. But that was before I realized that Monica was willing to overlook all my glaring personality flaws.

jokes.text: 'Last time you went out with her you said she was a dud! I judged her too quickly. This time, we took it to the next level.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is horrified that Chandler went out with Joanna again after previously dismissing her as a dud.
jokes.punchline: 'We took it to the next level' is a relationship euphemism that, given the context of Joanna being Rachel's boss, lands as both boastful and catastrophically misguided.
jokes.explanation: Functional exposition-comedy hybrid. The joke is that Chandler slept with someone he called a dud, and the euphemism lands mildly. Not particularly original but serves the plot.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, I spend most of my day at work doing... well, let's just say I'm very familiar with the inside of my office door. I've memorized every wood grain. I could describe the lock mechanism to a locksmith. I once spent twenty minutes watching dust particles float through the sunlight. That's not sad at all, right? No, completely normal. Most people probably do the same thing. Stare at walls. Count ceiling tiles. I'm at 247, by the way. I'll let you know when I hit 250. We'll celebrate. Just me and my office supplies.

jokes.text: 'It's not an everyday occurrence! Usually I'm in there by myself.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is appalled that Chandler slept with her boss Joanna.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's self-deprecating defense — that he usually has sex alone (implying masturbation) — is delivered deadpan and makes him seem pathetically lonely rather than villainous.
jokes.explanation: A solid Chandler self-deprecation about his sex life — or lack thereof. The joke works because his defense inadvertently makes him look worse. Good character specificity; this reads as authentically Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My boss kept saying how much he liked my... presentation skills.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Chandler, that's... I mean, that's not...

jokes.text: Ross's talking-head admission: 'Sorry. I knew what he meant.'
jokes.setup: Chandler says Joanna 'isn't just the boss in your office, if you know what I mean' — a lewd innuendo about sexual dominance.
jokes.punchline: Ross, in a confessional aside, admits he understood the sex joke perfectly — making his earlier straight-faced behavior funnier in retrospect.
jokes.explanation: A quick aside that works because of its brevity and the way it retroactively recontextualizes Ross's silence. The economy is excellent — five words doing the full job.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom, it's just nail polish. I like the color blue.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: Blue? Monica, you look like your grandmother after the funeral home couldn't get the formaldehyde stains out.

jokes.text: 'It's what your grandmother's hands looked like when we found her.'
jokes.setup: Monica is wearing blue nail polish, which she thinks is cute. Her mother Judy comments on it.
jokes.punchline: Judy compares Monica's fashion choice to a dead grandmother's post-mortem hands — a grotesque and casually cruel image delivered without apparent malice.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first standout joke. It works on multiple levels: it's dark (comparing a fashion choice to a corpse), it's character-specific (only Judy Geller would say this and think she's being helpful), and it's shockingly mean while being utterly deadpan. The specificity of 'when we found her' is what elevates it from dark to exceptional — the implication that the grandmother was 'found' rather than dying peacefully adds a whole extra layer of tragedy/comedy. Could only come from Judy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: A lesbian wedding? Well, at least you'll finally get to cater an event where the bride actually wants to be there.

jokes.text: Judy explains she hired Monica because of food at Richard's party — then immediately undercuts it: '...but you were sleeping with him.' Then adds the lesbian wedding caveat.
jokes.setup: Monica asks why Judy hired her. Judy starts with a compliment — she heard the food at Richard's party was great.
jokes.punchline: Judy immediately qualifies that Monica was sleeping with Richard, casting doubt on the objectivity of his endorsement, then adds the lesbian wedding — noting she assumes Monica didn't sleep with anyone there — as her only other data point.
jokes.explanation: Judy at her most devastatingly backhanded. The joke is structured as a compliment that keeps getting worse — each qualifier strips Monica of more dignity. The lesbian wedding reference adds absurdist escalation. Strong character integration: this is exactly how Judy operates.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Don't worry, Monica. I'm sure your catering will be great. I mean, just because it's for a lesbian wedding doesn't mean anything has to be different. Women like food just as much as men do!

jokes.text: 'At least that would be something.'
jokes.setup: Judy is cataloguing all the reasons she's uncertain about Monica's cooking credentials. She notes that at the lesbian wedding, she assumes Monica slept with no one.
jokes.punchline: 'At least that would be something' — Judy implies that Monica sleeping with a woman would at least be interesting, whereas Monica's actual life is not.
jokes.explanation: Brutally economical. Six words that summarize Judy's low opinion of Monica's life while being genuinely funny rather than just mean. The phrasing 'at least that would be something' implies Monica's entire existence is a disappointment. High economy score because the joke lands perfectly without a single wasted syllable.

dialogue.speaker: Encyclopedia Salesman
dialogue.line: Do you own a set of encyclopedias?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, I don't.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But you should try the building next door.

jokes.text: Monica's excited misreading: 'Oh, my God! Did you hear that? She hired me because she thinks I'm good!'
jokes.setup: Judy has just delivered a string of devastating backhanded assessments of Monica's cooking credentials.
jokes.punchline: Monica extracts the single positive fragment from Judy's monologue and ignores all the surrounding cruelty — showing both her desperation for her mother's approval and her selective hearing.
jokes.explanation: A strong character moment — Monica's need for validation is so acute she reframes a deeply insulting speech as a compliment. The joke is at her expense but with sympathy. Good character integration: this is Monica's central wound with her mother, handled with comic precision.

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Do you ever feel left out of conversations?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, all the time! So I've been working on my vocabulary. Like, I'll say things like 'that's a flagrant disregard for the Geneva Convention' or 'that's a Shakespearean tragedy.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The other day, Chandler was talking about some economic thing, and I said, 'Yeah, well, that's just like the stock market crash of 1929 — very Dickensian.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, the stock market crash happened in 1929, but Dickens died in 1870.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he's dead now!

jokes.text: 'And hey, it's cool if you're a lesbian.'
jokes.setup: Monica has had a genuine emotional reaction to her mother's backhanded hiring rationale. The scene has a moment of sincerity.
jokes.punchline: Ross breaks the emotional beat with an entirely irrelevant reassurance that Monica could be a lesbian — responding to Judy's earlier tangent rather than the actual emotional moment.
jokes.explanation: A good tension-breaker that characterizes Ross as someone who processes conversations slowly and misses the emotional beat. The irrelevance is the joke — he's still thinking about the lesbian wedding comment from two minutes ago.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, where's your nail?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? It broke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're a freak!

jokes.text: Encyclopedia salesman pitches Joey: 'Do your friends ever have a conversation and you just nod along, not sure what they're talking about?' — Joey immediately demonstrates this with the three friends mid-argument.
jokes.setup: The encyclopedia salesman delivers a pitch specifically designed for people who feel left out of conversations they don't understand.
jokes.punchline: The answer is immediately demonstrated visually as Joey's three friends have an animated conversation about things Joey clearly doesn't understand (Nobel Prize, Algonquin Round Table), and Joey has presumably been nodding along.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is elegant: the salesman's pitch is immediately answered by the surrounding scene, making the joke land on two levels simultaneously. The situational irony is that the perfect mark for encyclopedia sales is standing right there. Strong character integration — this is a fundamentally Joey situation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could buy new nails so no one will know.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, there's a nail in the food!

jokes.text: Three friends having an animated conversation: 'I'm telling you, it's totally unconstitutional.' / 'I think he deserves a Nobel Prize.' / 'It was like the Algonquin kids' table.'
jokes.setup: Joey's friends are having a conversation in the background while the salesman is pitching Joey.
jokes.punchline: The three snippets of conversation are deliberately mismatched — a Constitutional argument, a Nobel Prize opinion, and a reference to the Algonquin Round Table — suggesting they're talking completely past each other, or that their intellectual range is comically pretentious.
jokes.explanation: These three snippets work as background comedy — they're intentionally impenetrable to show why Joey would need encyclopedias. The Algonquin kids' table is the cleverest of the three. Functions well in context but is mostly a supporting joke to #18.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom, there's a nail in the quiche.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: A nail? Oh, how fun! It's like a surprise present in every bite!

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: I once served a casserole with a thumbtack in it. No one even noticed!

jokes.text: Monica missing a fake fingernail — 'Oh, my God! I had them when I put... Oh, my God! It's in the quiche!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe notices Monica has only nine fingernails after she put on fake ones to impress her mother.
jokes.punchline: Monica realizes a blue fake nail has been baked into the quiche she's serving at her mother's party.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed escalating cringe setup. The stakes are high (Monica's mother's party, her credibility), the problem is specific and visual (a blue nail), and the setup with the fake nails earlier pays off perfectly. Strong structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, you had backup lasagnas? How many lasagnas did you make?

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Well, I made three just in case.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: In case of what? In case I ruined the first one? In case I ruined the second one?

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: I just like to be prepared.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You made three lasagnas because you didn't think I could make one lasagna.

jokes.text: 'It's because they're going to eat... That's the problem.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests they buy a new set of nails so Monica will 'look great' — apparently missing that a nail is baked into food people will eat.
jokes.punchline: Monica has to explain, with barely-controlled panic, that the issue isn't her appearance but that guests will consume a fingernail.
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat that reveals Phoebe's loopy logic. Monica's exasperated clarification is funny because Phoebe's misunderstanding is so thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: So if things don't work out with Chandler, you'll have a backup plan, right?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom, I'm not going to have a backup plan.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: Well, you should. You know, in case you pull a Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pull a Monica? What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: Oh honey, it's what we call it in the family when you mess everything up and need therapy to deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's... that's a thing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: Of course it's a thing. We've been saying it for years.

jokes.text: 'Honey, don't bite your nails.' — Monica to Phoebe, who is anxiously chewing her nails during the crisis.
jokes.setup: A fake fingernail is lost in the quiche. Monica is in crisis mode.
jokes.punchline: In the midst of the crisis, Monica notices Phoebe biting her (real) nails — the very behavior that led to this problem — and instinctively scolds her.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful callback with perfect economy. Four words that simultaneously: reference the earlier setup, characterize Monica's controlling nature, and note the absurdity of the current crisis. The timing — mid-panic — makes it funnier. Monica's maternal instinct to correct behavior doesn't switch off even in emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, I have a sense of humor about myself. I just don't think it's funny that I'm not funny.

jokes.text: 'And there's no way to know which one.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just told her mother there's a blue fingernail in one of the quiche cups.
jokes.punchline: The additional detail — that it could be in any one of them — escalates the disaster. The delivery, presumably matter-of-fact, makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A clean escalation beat. The joke is in the additional information — it's not just one contaminated quiche, it could be any of them. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mother
dialogue.line: I have faith in you, Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mom, look around! There are dirty dishes in the sink, there's dust on the shelves, and I haven't vacuumed in weeks!

jokes.text: 'And whoever finds it wins the prize!'
jokes.setup: Monica has just horrified the guests by announcing a fingernail is in an unspecified quiche.
jokes.punchline: Monica's nervous improvisation — framing the disaster as a game — is both panicked and brilliantly Monica (trying to manage a disaster through cheerful social engineering).
jokes.explanation: Monica in full crisis-management mode, pivoting from transparency to game-show hostess. The line is unexpected, perfectly character-specific (only Monica would try this), and lands as both a great in-character choice and a great joke. The audience would love this — high impact.

dialogue.speaker: Joanna
dialogue.line: So we're really breaking up?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes. I'm very sad about this.

jokes.text: Judy's reaction: 'Why are you laughing? Now your father owes me $5.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just announced a fingernail-in-quiche disaster at Judy's party. Someone (presumably Jack) is laughing.
jokes.punchline: Judy reveals she and Jack had a side bet that something would go wrong — and this vindicates her.
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Judy and Jack bet on Monica's failure is devastating and perfectly character-consistent. It recontextualizes the whole catering arrangement as a setup for parental sport. Strong character integration — this is exactly the kind of thing Judy Geller would do.

dialogue.speaker: Joanna
dialogue.line: Why are you getting dressed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, they won't let me back in the office without clothes. Apparently, I can't just come to work in my underwear anymore. Something about 'professional standards' and 'making people uncomfortable.' I tried to explain that I'm doing them a favor—I'm a lot less attractive with clothes on.

jokes.text: 'Don't be silly. I just bet that I'd need these.' / She produces frozen lasagnas.
jokes.setup: Monica, hurt, asks if Judy bet she'd lose a nail (i.e., screw up).
jokes.punchline: Judy has backup frozen lasagnas ready to go — she came so prepared for Monica's failure that she brought a contingency meal.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The image of Judy Geller arriving at her own party with backup lasagnas in case her daughter failed is both hysterically cruel and extremely specific to this character. The escalation from 'I bet you'd fail' to 'I brought physical backup meals' is perfectly structured. The lasagnas become a recurring comedic object through the rest of the episode, giving this a strong structural bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Joanna
dialogue.line: Put your hands together.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh! I thought you said put your pants together.

jokes.text: 'This was just in case you "pulled a Monica".'
jokes.setup: Judy is explaining the backup lasagnas.
jokes.punchline: Judy uses the phrase 'pulled a Monica' — implying Monica's name has become synonymous with screwing things up, even within her own family.
jokes.explanation: The introduction of 'pulling a Monica' as a phrase is the episode's central comedic conceit and this is its most devastating use. Coming from Monica's own mother, it's genuinely shocking in its cruelty. The phrase is inherently quotable and becomes the engine for the episode's thematic comedy. High originality because inventing a character-named idiom for failure is a clever structural device.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Where am I supposed to put it?

jokes.text: 'You promised Dr. Weinberg you'd never use that phrase.'
jokes.setup: Judy has just used the phrase 'pulled a Monica' to mean screwing up.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals that the phrase is so established and so hurtful that it came up in therapy — and her mother promised her psychiatrist she wouldn't use it.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation of the 'pulled a Monica' joke. The revelation that it was banned by a therapist means: (a) it's been used before, repeatedly, (b) Monica was damaged enough to bring it to therapy, and (c) Judy agreed to stop and immediately violated that agreement. Layers of cruelty packed into one line.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't come back right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm in a tunnel.

jokes.text: 'That's right. My mom has no faith in me! That's hilarious!'
jokes.setup: Judy tells Monica to have a sense of humor and notes she's never able to laugh at herself.
jokes.punchline: Monica tries to perform laughing at herself while clearly being devastated — the performance of forced hilarity while in pain is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat. Monica's inability to actually laugh at herself while being told she can't laugh at herself is a neat ironic loop. Works in the room due to Courteney Cox's physical performance.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rachel, could you unlock these handcuffs?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How did you get handcuffed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's not important. But while you're here, has anyone ever told you that you have the most beautiful eyes in the entire world?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And your hair! My God, your hair is like spun gold!

jokes.text: 'No. You have lasagnas!'
jokes.setup: Judy claims she does have faith in Monica.
jokes.punchline: Monica points to the backup lasagnas as physical evidence of Judy's lack of faith — the lasagnas have become a symbol of her mother's low expectations.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — four words that serve as both a devastating comeback and a thematic button. 'You have lasagnas' works as a punchline because the lasagnas have already been established as a metaphor for Judy's lack of faith. High quotability because the phrase lands so cleanly and could become shorthand for 'your actions contradict your words.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You didn't break up with her?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, technically I did. I said 'I think we should see other people.' That's breaking up.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, she's still your girlfriend!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, she didn't say she agreed with me!

jokes.text: Phoebe announces: 'The ruined quiches are ready!'
jokes.setup: The quiche situation is a disaster — one has a fingernail in it.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe cheerfully announces them as 'ruined quiches' the way a chef would announce a finished dish — normalizing the disaster.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's sunny obliviousness applied to catastrophic circumstances. The joke is in the cheerful delivery of objectively bad news. 'The ruined quiches are ready!' has the cadence of a triumphant announcement, making the modifier all the funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Did it ever enter your mind that you were jeopardizing my career?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, there are a lot of things that enter my mind, but I try not to act on all of them.

jokes.text: Chandler and Joanna 'breaking up' scene: 'It just doesn't feel like we're breaking up.' / 'No, we are. I'm sad.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has promised to break up with Joanna. He's now executing the breakup.
jokes.punchline: Joanna notes it doesn't feel like a breakup; Chandler confirms it is, citing his sadness with flat affect — underplaying emotion to comic effect.
jokes.explanation: A mild but functional joke. 'No, we are. I'm sad.' is classic Chandler deadpan — the flatness of the self-reported sadness is funnier than any emotional performance would be.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Get yourself out of the handcuffs.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh sure, I'll just use my amazing powers of magic.

jokes.text: 'When I walk outside naked, people throw garbage.'
jokes.setup: Joanna asks what Chandler is doing (getting dressed). He explains why he gets dressed to leave.
jokes.punchline: The reason given — people throw garbage at him when he's naked outside — is delivered as a matter-of-fact complaint about a recurring experience.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. The setup is mundane (why are you getting dressed?) and the answer is absurdly specific and self-deprecating. 'People throw garbage' implies it's happened enough times to be a known pattern. The deadpan delivery of a surreal situation is very much in Chandler's wheelhouse but the specific imagery elevates it. High originality and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Give me back my Walkman!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, but hear me out. What if I just... borrow it for one more day?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No! Give it back now!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Fine, fine. What if I keep it for two more days, and in return, I'll... do your laundry?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. Three days, I'll do your laundry AND make you lunch for a week.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's it, I'm calling Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait! How about forever, and I buy you a new, better Walkman? A Discman even!

jokes.text: 'You're not the boss of me.' — beat — 'Yeah, you are.'
jokes.setup: Joanna is about to handcuff Chandler, and he begins to resist with the reflexive retort 'You're not the boss of me.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately remembers that she is, literally, the boss of Rachel — who is his friend — and corrects himself.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured two-line joke. The self-correction mid-sentence is perfectly timed and the brevity is impeccable. The joke works on character logic (Chandler realizing his power position), on wordplay (boss/boss), and on comedic rhythm. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do your wrists hurt?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, they would if I hadn't gotten so good at getting out of handcuffs.

jokes.text: Saucy!
jokes.setup: Chandler concedes Joanna is the boss of him after she produces handcuffs.
jokes.punchline: Joanna's single-word response — 'Saucy!' — delivered with exactly the right amount of camp — is funnier for its brevity and period-specific cheekiness than any longer line could be.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word delivers the whole joke. 'Saucy!' as a reaction to Chandler's submission is perfectly calibrated in its archaic campiness. Works purely through tone and brevity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I couldn't come in today because... my grandmother died.

dialogue.speaker: Joanna
dialogue.line: Oh Chandler, I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she's going to be really upset she missed work.

jokes.text: 'If you don't come back soon... there's pretty much nothing I can do about it!'
jokes.setup: Joanna has left Chandler handcuffed to her chair and gone to her boss's car, saying she'll be back in two minutes.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mock-threat is immediately undercut by his acknowledgment of his own helplessness — he's trying to sound intimidating but has no leverage whatsoever.
jokes.explanation: Self-aware humor at its best — Chandler venting a threat and immediately acknowledging it's empty. The rhythm works well, and the self-correction mirrors joke #35. Good Chandler characterization of someone who narrates his own helplessness.

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Did you know Van Gogh only sold one painting in his lifetime?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow. So... he really struggled, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Yes, he was very poor and—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I got it. Van Gogh: poor guy, didn't sell paintings. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Well, he also cut off his own ear—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. That's a whole different thing.

jokes.text: Rachel enters with a macaroon: 'I brought you back a macaroon.' Chandler, handcuffed: 'Great. I'll keep it in my butt with your nose.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has casually walked in with a macaroon for Chandler, apparently not registering the handcuff situation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response is surreal and slightly crude — 'I'll keep it in my butt with your nose' is an absurdist insult that escalates from confusion to controlled rage.
jokes.explanation: The line is inventively surreal — it's an insult construction that's odd enough to be funny on its own terms. The casual delivery of 'I'll keep it in my butt' while Chandler is handcuffed and furious is good cringe/absurdist comedy. Slightly crude but earned by the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't get it. Why would he cut off his ear? If I really loved my girlfriend, I'd buy her a nice present, not mutilate myself.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Besides, what's she gonna do with an ear? It's not like she can wear it.

jokes.text: 'That's weird. She locked the door.' / 'You know why? She's got the bonus list in there.'
jokes.setup: Sophie and a coworker try to get into Joanna's office (where Chandler is handcuffed) and find it locked.
jokes.punchline: The coworker's confident explanation — the bonus list — is the mundane workplace explanation that the audience knows is wildly wrong, creating ironic tension.
jokes.explanation: A functional irony joke — the gap between what the coworker thinks is in the locked office and what's actually in there (Chandler, handcuffed). Works as dramatic irony but isn't especially clever.

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: So Joey, who's the head of the Catholic Church?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The Pope.

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Right. And what do you call a large furry animal that lives in the woods?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A bear?

dialogue.speaker: Salesman
dialogue.line: Exactly. So what's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: One wears a funny hat?

jokes.text: Coworker reveals Mark gave her a key to Joanna's office: 'You want to see the list?'
jokes.setup: Coworker has a secret key to Joanna's office.
jokes.punchline: She offers to use it to see the bonus list — which means opening the door to reveal Chandler handcuffed to the chair, though she doesn't know it yet.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the office discovery scene. More of a plot beat than a joke, but the anticipation of what they're about to find gives it comedic value as dramatic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Vulcanized? Like the Vulcans from Star Trek?

jokes.text: 'And on a totally separate subject, that's a lovely pantsuit.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just asked Rachel (who has come to the office) to grab the keys and unlock him, after she discovered him handcuffed.
jokes.punchline: He awkwardly pivots to a compliment about her pantsuit, hoping flattery will soften the ask — the 'totally separate subject' framing is nakedly transparent.
jokes.explanation: 'On a totally separate subject' is a great construction — it's the kind of obvious pivot that's funny because of how badly it's disguised. Strong economy and the panic beneath the flattery is well-characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! You know what? We could start a new thing where 'pulling a Monica' means doing something really smart and organized!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah! Like, 'Oh, I totally pulled a Monica and color-coded my sock drawer by thread count!'

jokes.text: 'I did break up with her! She just took it really, really well!'
jokes.setup: Rachel accuses Chandler of not breaking up with Joanna as promised.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's defense — that the breakup happened but Joanna 'took it really, really well' — is obviously undermined by his current handcuffed situation.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured irony joke. The phrase 'took it really, really well' is doing dark comedic work — she took it so well she cuffed him to a chair. The double 'really' suggests Chandler is aware of how absurd his position is.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? We should start using 'pulling a Monica' as a compliment. Like when someone cleans up after themselves or organizes something really well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? I like that.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah! Like, 'Oh my God, I totally pulled a Monica and color-coded my spice rack by cuisine and alphabetical order.'

jokes.text: 'You got yourself into those cuffs, you get yourself out.' / 'I can't get myself right out of them. You must have me confused with the "Amazing Chandler"!'
jokes.setup: Rachel refuses to help Chandler, telling him to get out of the cuffs himself.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's indignant response invoking 'the Amazing Chandler' as a fictional escape-artist alter ego is a surreal piece of self-branding that implies he normally gets into these situations.
jokes.explanation: 'The Amazing Chandler' is a funny piece of invented mythology — the name has the right pomposity for an escape artist while being obviously non-existent. The joke works because the outrage is perfectly calibrated: Chandler's dignity is wounded that Rachel would expect him to escape on his own.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: See, that's what I'm talking about. They rebrand everything. 'New Coke,' 'New Diet Coke,' 'Coke Zero'... it's all just Coke!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And don't even get me started on 'The Learning Channel.' It's not about learning anymore, it's about watching people hoard stuff and fight their families.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But baseball... baseball stays the same. Batter up! There's a fastball on the inside corner. He swings and... it's a fly ball to left field. The outfielder is moving back... back... he's got it!

jokes.text: The negotiation: 'Never see her again. Never!' / 'Never come in here again.' / 'Fine!' / 'Give me back my Walkman!'
jokes.setup: Rachel uses Chandler's helplessness to extract promises — he'll never see Joanna again, never come to the office.
jokes.punchline: The demands escalate absurdly to 'give me back my Walkman' — a petty grievance that has apparently been festering, now brought out as leverage.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation comedy — the demands start reasonable (stop seeing Joanna) and devolve into petty personal grievances (the Walkman). The sudden pivot to the Walkman is funny because it suggests Rachel has been waiting for an opportunity to address this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can crack walnuts with my breasts.

jokes.text: 'I never borrowed it.' / 'Then I lost it. Buy me one!'
jokes.setup: Rachel demands Chandler return her Walkman as part of the handcuff negotiation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler denies borrowing it; Rachel's immediate pivot — 'then I lost it, buy me one' — reveals that the Walkman is a pretext and she just wants compensation regardless of fault.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's negotiating tactics are hilariously dishonest — the logic 'then I lost it, buy me one' is absurd but delivered with total confidence. Good character moment for Rachel as an opportunist.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, the last time you cleaned a bathroom, I found a Cheeto behind the toilet.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That was... a decorative Cheeto.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It had mold on it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Vintage.

jokes.text: 'Does it hurt?' / 'No, I always see guys do this when handcuffs are taken off.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has unlocked Chandler and is watching him rub his wrists.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's sarcastic response implies that wrist-rubbing is a signature move of men who've been handcuffed — absurd and self-deprecating simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: A solid Chandler quip that works through absurd specificity. The idea that he's observed 'guys' doing this implies a rich, inexplicable familiarity with handcuff removal protocol.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more desperate?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Here boy, here boy! Please, I'm begging you!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Sit!

jokes.text: 'She'll know I have a key to her office. I've got to lock you back up.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been freed by Rachel. Rachel suddenly realizes that if Joanna returns and finds Chandler gone, she'll know Rachel was in the office with a key.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's solution is to re-handcuff Chandler to preserve her cover — sacrificing him to save herself.
jokes.explanation: A great escalation beat — just when Chandler is free, Rachel's self-interest creates a new complication. The logic is sound (Rachel's explanation makes sense) which makes it funnier. Good character moment for Rachel as someone who prioritizes herself.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did you know that vomit can travel up to 27 feet? I just learned that. And honestly, it's not something you want to know. It's one of those things where ignorance is bliss. But now I know. So that's great.

jokes.text: Joey's encyclopedia conversation: 'He cut off his ear.' / 'And?' / 'I'm out.' / 'He painted that.' / 'That's pretty nice. I thought he cut off his ear because he sucked.'
jokes.setup: The salesman asks Joey what he knows about Van Gogh.
jokes.punchline: Joey knows Van Gogh cut off his ear but has no idea why — and his theory (that he cut it off because he sucked at painting) is both wrong and somehow endearing.
jokes.explanation: A strong Joey ignorance joke with a twist — 'I thought he cut off his ear because he sucked' is a genuinely funny misinterpretation that has its own internal logic. The 'I'm out' after just one fact is perfectly Joey. High character integration — this joke could only come from Joey's specific brand of confident ignorance.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A thousand two hundred dollars?! For books?! Do I look like a guy who has a thousand two hundred dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't even afford the 'D' volume!

jokes.text: I thought he cut off his ear because he sucked.
jokes.setup: The customer reveals Van Gogh painted 'that' (presumably a famous work).
jokes.punchline: Joey's casual reinterpretation of Van Gogh's self-mutilation as a critical self-assessment is accidentally profound in its wrongness — and the delivery would be total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Joey's art criticism — that Van Gogh cut off his ear as a self-review of his own work — is the kind of absurdist logic that reveals perfect character. It's high-concept in its simplicity, highly quotable, and could only come from Joey. The economy ('because he sucked') is excellent. Strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look what I found in my pockets today. A gum wrapper, three pennies, a button that's not from any of my shirts, and what I think used to be a sandwich.

jokes.text: 'Where does the Pope live?' / 'In the woods.'
jokes.setup: The salesman is testing Joey's general knowledge with encyclopedia-level questions.
jokes.punchline: Joey's answer — 'in the woods' — conflates 'Pope' with a bear (from the joke 'Does a bear shit in the woods?'), suggesting his knowledge storage is chaotically organized.
jokes.explanation: A great short joke. 'In the woods' is unexpected and the implication (Joey has confused the Pope with a bear or has no idea) is funnier than any long explanation. The salesman's 'Wait, that's the joke answer' makes the confusion explicit without over-explaining. High economy, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at all this money I found!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... these aren't my clothes.

jokes.text: Salesman corrects Joey: 'Actually, it's Vatican City.' Then: 'Now, what do you know about vulcanized rubber?'
jokes.setup: Having corrected Joey on the Pope, the salesman moves to the next topic: vulcanized rubber.
jokes.punchline: Joey's answer: 'Spock's birth control.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke in the Joey storyline. 'Spock's birth control' is three words that: (1) completely misidentify vulcanized rubber by conflating 'vulcanized' with 'Vulcan' (Spock's species), (2) add the non sequitur of birth control, and (3) are delivered with total Joey confidence. The word-association logic is clear enough to follow but the destination is gloriously wrong. High originality, perfect economy, quintessential Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I can't wait to see what happens next! Do you think Ross will finally tell Rachel how he feels?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait... it says here that the Earth revolves around the sun. I did NOT see that coming!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is better than the movies! Volume V, baby! The plot thickens!

jokes.text: Wait, that's the joke answer. Actually, it's Vatican City.
jokes.setup: Joey said the Pope lives in the woods.
jokes.punchline: Joey corrects himself — as if 'in the woods' was the joke answer he meant to give, not his real answer — before providing the correct answer with the casual authority of someone who is definitely not working from the encyclopedias he's holding.
jokes.explanation: The recovery is almost better than the initial joke. Joey's seamless pivot from 'in the woods' to 'Vatican City' — pretending it was a joke all along — shows exactly the kind of self-preserving BS that makes Joey so funny. The confidence of the delivery would be the key.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to tell everyone about your... situation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What situation?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Let's just say when you go to the bathroom, even the tiles feel inadequate.

jokes.text: 'You need these books.'
jokes.setup: The salesman has just heard 'Spock's birth control' as Joey's answer about vulcanized rubber.
jokes.punchline: The salesman's flat, defeated conclusion — 'You need these books' — is a perfect straight-man button. His prior skepticism about making a sale has evaporated; now he's pitching out of genuine concern.
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly placed. The salesman shifting from salesperson to concerned citizen is the joke — 'You need these books' has the gravity of a doctor delivering a diagnosis. The economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to make you a legend.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How? By telling people that Milton Berle's is small next to mine?

jokes.text: 'This used to be your room? You must have been in really good shape as a kid.'
jokes.setup: Monica shows Phoebe her childhood room at her mother's house (presumably now a gym or exercise room).
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's observation that a child living there would be in excellent shape implies the room has been converted to a gym — Monica's mother has literally replaced her daughter's bedroom with exercise equipment.
jokes.explanation: A clever visual joke inferred from Phoebe's line — Judy has converted Monica's childhood room into a gym, which is another layer of maternal rejection. Phoebe's innocent observation lands as dark comedy about Judy's parenting priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What would make you proud? If I had a successful catering business?

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: Well, that would be wonderful, but I was thinking more along the lines of you getting married and having children.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is my catering business will never be successful enough.

dialogue.speaker: Monica's Mom
dialogue.line: No, that's not what I'm saying at all.

jokes.text: Monica's crisis: 'I'm such an idiot! I can't believe I thought she could change.' / Ross: 'Who cares what your mom thinks? So you "pulled a Monica".'
jokes.setup: Monica is devastated by her mother's lack of faith (as evidenced by the backup lasagnas).
jokes.punchline: Ross uses the phrase 'pulled a Monica' — which was previously established as a painful insult — in what he thinks is a supportive context, completely missing why it's hurtful.
jokes.explanation: The phrase's second major use — Ross deploying it with brotherly affection while completely missing its sting. Good callback structure that deepens the joke by showing the phrase is now loose in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica, your catering business is doing so well! You're like, totally killing it!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Thanks, Phoebe. I've been working really hard.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, seriously, you're absolutely crushing it! You're crushing it so hard right now!

jokes.text: Ross's plan to rehabilitate the phrase: 'Just change what it means. Prove your mother wrong. You finish the job, and we'll call that "pulling a Monica".'
jokes.setup: Monica is hurt that 'pulling a Monica' means screwing up. Ross tries to help.
jokes.punchline: Ross proposes a grassroots rebranding campaign — if Monica succeeds, they'll reclaim the phrase. The plan is earnest but oblivious to how language actually works.
jokes.explanation: A charming Ross moment — his attempt to help is sweet but the plan is absurdly overoptimistic. Good setup for the escalating examples that follow.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for saying that. The lasagna was actually... well, it was the backup lasagna.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The first one kind of... didn't make it. But nobody could tell the difference!

jokes.text: Ross: 'If a kid gets straight A's, his parents say, "You pulled a Monica".' / 'A fireman saves a baby, and they go, "He pulled a Monica".' / 'Someone hits a homer, and they say, "That one's out of here".' / 'Because some things don't change.'
jokes.setup: Ross is enthusiastically selling Monica on his plan to reclaim the phrase 'pulling a Monica' to mean excellence.
jokes.punchline: The third example breaks the pattern — Ross runs out of steam on the baseball scenario and defaults to the actual baseball expression, then philosophically concludes 'some things don't change' — acknowledging the plan won't work.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest structural jokes. The rule of three is perfectly deployed: two examples of the new usage, then a collapse into the real phrase, then a philosophical button that's almost profound. 'Some things don't change' works as both a punchline and a genuine observation. Ross's unconscious abandonment of his own plan in the third example is brilliant character comedy — he convinces himself of the plan's failure mid-pitch. High marks across all dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can get out of these handcuffs!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, you can't.

jokes.text: Someone hits a homer, and they say, 'That one's out of here'. / Because some things don't change.
jokes.setup: Rachel keeps trying to redefine 'pulled a Monica' with positive examples.
jokes.punchline: Monica's baseball deflation — noting that home runs already have their own expression, and some things just can't be rebranded — is a perfect comedic landing for the running gag.
jokes.explanation: An excellent punchline for the running gag sequence. Monica's baseball counterexample isn't just a joke — it punctures Rachel's optimism with precise logic. 'Because some things don't change' is a great button: funny, self-aware, and slightly heartbreaking.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Vesuvius? Oh yeah, that's a volcano. It erupted in 79 A.D. and buried Pompeii. I read about it in this encyclopedia I got.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm not just a pretty face, you know. I'm expanding my mind.

jokes.text: 'My breasts are really strong.'
jokes.setup: Monica is psyching herself up to go back in and serve the food she actually made rather than the backup lasagnas.
jokes.punchline: Her affirmation of choice is 'my breasts are really strong' — seemingly a non sequitur until you realize she's referring to her strength of character ('breasts' as metonym for physical/emotional toughness in this context), or possibly a cooking reference (chicken breasts?). The ambiguity makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A delightfully weird line that works through ambiguity. Whether she means her literal breasts (nonsensical), a cooking metaphor (chicken breasts in the casserole?), or is just genuinely odd, the non sequitur nature of the line in a moment of self-encouragement is funny. High economy — four words that do a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, since when are you an expert on volcanoes?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not just about volcanoes, Mon. I know about Vikings, violins, vitamins, volleyball, ventriloquism, vacuums, and... Vegas!

jokes.text: Rachel's escalating handcuff negotiation: 'I'll clean your bathroom for a month.' / 'Still won't be clean.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to negotiate with Chandler to get him to agree to being re-cuffed.
jokes.punchline: Chandler rejects 'I'll clean your bathroom' as a bribe because he knows Rachel's cleaning standards are so low it won't matter.
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp character comedy. 'Still won't be clean' is dismissive and funny — it's a dig at Rachel's domestic habits that lands quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, in Korea, like, everybody's name is Kim. It's like, how do they even know who they're talking to?

jokes.text: Rachel's bribe escalation: 'Foot rubs for a month!' / 'Freedom!' / 'I'll put all your photos into albums!' / 'I want my freedom!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is desperately offering increasingly domestic bribes; Chandler keeps responding with one word: 'Freedom!'
jokes.punchline: The contrast between Rachel's increasingly specific domestic offers (foot rubs, photo albums) and Chandler's escalating Braveheart-style cry for freedom creates a comedic mismatch.
jokes.explanation: The escalating bribe-vs-freedom exchange works because the juxtaposition is absurd — Rachel is offering photo album organization while Chandler is invoking existential liberty. The repetition of 'Freedom!' builds comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Joanna
dialogue.line: Well, this is a little awkward.

jokes.text: 'Why won't you hear me! Sophie, help me!' / 'Sophie, sit!'
jokes.setup: Rachel appeals to Sophie (a coworker) for help in the negotiation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler commands Sophie to 'sit' like a dog — dismissing her as irrelevant to his freedom demands with a patronizing command.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the escalation sequence. 'Sophie, sit!' is a funny power move from someone who is literally handcuffed — the authority is entirely unearned but delivered with conviction.

jokes.text: 'There's a lot I didn't know about vomit.'
jokes.setup: Joanna has apparently vomited (implied by the scene gap and Chandler's line).
jokes.punchline: Chandler's philosophical takeaway — delivered as a reflection on his newly expanded knowledge — is perfectly deadpan and absurdly understated given the circumstances.
jokes.explanation: Eight words of perfect deadpan. Chandler has apparently been educated about vomit in an up-close and unwanted way, and his response is philosophical rather than disgusted. The delivery — 'there's a lot I didn't know' as if he's emerging from a seminar — is very Chandler and very funny. High quotability.

jokes.text: Joey considers buying encyclopedias: 'What can you swing?' / 'How about zero down and zero a month for a long, long time?'
jokes.setup: The salesman asks Joey what payment he can manage for the $1200 encyclopedia set.
jokes.punchline: Joey proposes zero down and zero per month — i.e., he wants them for free — delivered as though this is a reasonable offer.
jokes.explanation: Good Joey comedy — he treats 'zero down, zero a month' as a legitimate financial proposal. The 'for a long, long time' qualifier makes it funnier — he's not even offering a future payment date.

jokes.text: $1200? / You think I have $1200? I'm home during the day and I got patio furniture in my living room.
jokes.setup: Joey gives the encyclopedia pitch price of $1200.
jokes.punchline: The customer's defense — 'I'm home during the day and I got patio furniture in my living room' — is a perfect self-aware declaration of financial status via two specific, mundane details.
jokes.explanation: The customer's self-diagnosis via 'home during the day' plus 'patio furniture in my living room' is an oddly specific and very funny portrait of genteel poverty. The specificity of patio furniture as a class signifier is the joke's best asset.

jokes.text: How about zero down and zero a month for a long, long time?
jokes.setup: Joey asks what the customer can 'swing' on payment.
jokes.punchline: The customer's counter-offer — zero down, zero a month, indefinitely — is so perfectly delusional in its framing as a legitimate payment plan that it's genuinely funny.
jokes.explanation: The framing of 'zero for a long, long time' as a payment plan is great absurdist humor. The earnestness of 'for a long, long time' is the kicker — she's not joking, she genuinely thinks this is reasonable. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Joey empties his pockets: 'a baby Tootsie Roll, a movie stub, keys, a Kleenex... a rock... and an army man.'
jokes.setup: The salesman asks what Joey actually has as assets. Joey empties his pockets.
jokes.punchline: Joey's worldly possessions include a baby Tootsie Roll, a rock, and an army man — the pocket contents of a nine-year-old. The pause before 'a rock' suggests he presents it with the same gravity as a financial asset.
jokes.explanation: The specific inventory of Joey's pockets is the joke — each item is more childlike than the last, culminating in 'an army man.' The escalation from movie stub (normal) to Kleenex (somewhat normal) to rock (odd) to army man (pure child) is well-structured. High character integration — this is Joey's soul made tangible.

jokes.text: 'And a fifty. These must be Chandler's pants.'
jokes.setup: The salesman has given up on Joey after seeing his pocket contents. Then Joey finds a fifty-dollar bill.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately attributes the money to Chandler's pants — i.e., he's wearing his roommate's pants and didn't know — which says everything about Joey's lifestyle without a word of explanation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'These must be Chandler's pants' does triple duty: it explains the $50 (which Joey didn't earn), reveals Joey doesn't know whose pants he's wearing, and implies a roommate relationship so casual that pants-sharing goes unnoticed. Six words of perfect character comedy. The specificity — not 'I borrowed money' but 'these must be Chandler's pants' — is exceptional.

jokes.text: 'I'll stick with the V. I want to see how this bad boy turns out.'
jokes.setup: The salesman offers Joey one book for $50 and gives him a choice of any letter.
jokes.punchline: Joey chooses 'V' — the letter of the volume he's been discussing (vulcanized rubber) — framing an encyclopedia volume as a page-turner he can't put down.
jokes.explanation: 'I want to see how this bad boy turns out' treats an encyclopedia volume like a suspenseful novel. Joey's genuine excitement about learning what vulcanized rubber is demonstrates his intellectual curiosity is real, just misdirected. Great character conclusion to his storyline.

jokes.text: Rachel's escalating bribe list: 'I will buy and wrap all of your Christmas gifts!' / 'I'll squeeze you fresh orange juice every morning!' / 'With extra pulp?'
jokes.setup: Rachel is desperately bribing Chandler to cooperate with being re-cuffed.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's negotiating counter — asking for extra pulp as if this is the deciding factor — is a great deadpan counter-offer. He's treating a hostage negotiation like an orange juice order.
jokes.explanation: 'With extra pulp?' as the negotiating pivot is a great comedic beat — Chandler treats orange juice pulp content as the make-or-break term of a high-stakes negotiation. Good economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: Rachel's scheme: 'I've got it!' / 'You don't have it.' / 'I have so got it!'
jokes.setup: Rachel thinks she has a solution to the Joanna problem.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's preemptive 'You don't have it' — before Rachel has even explained her plan — implies he knows Rachel well enough to know her schemes don't work.
jokes.explanation: Good character-based predictive comedy. Chandler's dismissal before the explanation is funny because it's based on genuine knowledge of Rachel's track record. The exchange rhythm — got it / don't have it / have so got it — is crisp.

jokes.text: When they ask me what I saw, I can be very generous... or very stingy.
jokes.setup: Rachel is leveraging the fact that Monica, Phoebe and Sophie know about Chandler's situation.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's pause between 'generous' and 'or very stingy' — implying she controls the narrative about what she 'saw' in terms of Chandler's physical state/situation — is a confident power play played for comedy.
jokes.explanation: The pause structure ('generous... or very stingy') is the joke's engine. It works because the implication (generous/stingy in her description of Chandler's physical attributes) is understood without being stated. Rachel suddenly having power is a nice character reversal.

jokes.text: 'I can make you a legend. I can make you this generation's Milton Berle.' / 'And Milton Berle has...' / 'Not compared to you.'
jokes.setup: Rachel claims she can make Chandler 'a legend' by controlling what she tells people about what she saw.
jokes.punchline: The Milton Berle reference invokes his legendary anatomical reputation. Rachel confirms Chandler's is superior before he even finishes the question — the punchline is in the confirmation.
jokes.explanation: The Milton Berle joke is a well-known Hollywood legend reference that plays to comedy-savvy audiences. Rachel's 'Not compared to you' is a brilliant stroke — she confirms it before Chandler can finish the question, and her certainty (from having seen him handcuffed, presumably with less clothing) makes it both flattering and absurd. Good impact score because it's a crowd-pleaser.

jokes.text: 'It's hard to believe a while ago this was just ingredients.'
jokes.setup: Monica's dish has been well-received. Phoebe offers what she thinks is a profound observation about food.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's amazement that food is made of ingredients — a self-evident truth she delivers as an epiphany — is quintessential Phoebe airheadedness.
jokes.explanation: A quietly brilliant Phoebe line. Her observation that food was 'just ingredients' is technically true and completely meaningless — but she says it with the wonder of someone who has just understood the nature of the universe. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: 'A bitch?' / 'I meant "wrong", but we can use your word.'
jokes.setup: Judy is grudgingly acknowledging that Monica succeeded. She leads Monica to complete the sentence: if everyone liked it and she liked it, that would make Monica...
jokes.punchline: Monica fills in 'bitch' — projecting her anger at her mother. Judy's response — 'I meant wrong, but we can use your word' — is deadpan perfection, accepting Monica's hostility with an aristocratic wave.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The structure is perfect: Judy sets up a fill-in-the-blank that should end with 'wrong,' Monica's rage takes over and she blurts 'bitch,' and Judy's utterly unflappable 'we can use your word' response is both a comeback and a character statement. Judy's composure in the face of being called a bitch — treating it as a reasonable vocabulary choice — is funnier than any defensive response would have been. This is Judy Geller at peak Judy Geller.

jokes.text: Phoebe (to Judy): 'You might even say that she "pulled a Monica".'
jokes.setup: Judy is grudgingly praising Monica's success.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe uses 'pulled a Monica' to mean success — exactly as Ross proposed — in front of Judy, who originated the phrase as an insult. The phrase has already been reclaimed.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff. The phrase that was used as Monica's epitaph of failure is now used in her moment of triumph, in front of her mother. Phoebe deploying it innocently (she doesn't know the full history of the phrase's devastation) adds an extra layer. Strong structural payoff.

jokes.text: 'She doesn't know we switched it.'
jokes.setup: Judy has praised Monica's food. Monica is touched.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals — apparently not quietly — that they switched Judy's backup lasagna with Monica's dish, meaning Judy's praise is for food she thought was Monica's, but the circumstances of the switch are now complicated.
jokes.explanation: A functional aside that somewhat undercuts the emotional resolution while adding a beat of Phoebe's obliviousness. Works as a character moment.

jokes.text: Judy's final threat: '...there will be nothing but ice in the freezer.'
jokes.setup: Judy has offered Monica future catering work, but she adds a condition.
jokes.punchline: Judy promises that next time there will be no backup lasagnas — she'll leave the freezer empty of emergency food. It's a threat that implies she'll hold Monica to a higher standard, delivered as a kind of backhanded compliment.
jokes.explanation: A strong callback button on the lasagna thread. 'Nothing but ice in the freezer' is Judy's version of a vote of confidence — she won't prepare for Monica's failure next time. It's simultaneously a compliment and a threat, which is perfect Judy characterization.

jokes.text: 'Mom, don't bite your nails!'
jokes.setup: Monica has just had a warm moment with her mother.
jokes.punchline: Monica catches her mother biting her nails — the habit that started the whole fingernail-in-quiche disaster — and reflexively scolds her, completing the running gag.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful full-circle callback. Monica catching her mother biting nails — the very behavior that created the episode's central crisis — and scolding her closes multiple loops simultaneously: the nail gag, Monica's relationship with her mother, and Monica's controlling nature. The economy is near-perfect (five words), the callback is tight, and it lands in a moment of genuine warmth making it both funny and touching. One of the episode's best structural jokes.

jokes.text: Joanna opens her office door to see Chandler still handcuffed: 'Hello, Chandler.' / 'I love you.'
jokes.setup: Joanna returns to her office to find Chandler still handcuffed to the chair.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, in a state of total resignation and defeat, greets her with 'I love you' — a declaration that has nothing to do with romance and everything to do with his desperation to be unchained.
jokes.explanation: The 'I love you' as a hostage-negotiation opener is a great character moment. Chandler has abandoned all dignity and gone straight to emotional manipulation. The timing — immediately upon seeing her — suggests he's been rehearsing it. High impact in a studio audience.

jokes.text: Joey's reaction: 'No, he doesn't!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has said 'I love you' to Joanna. Joey hears this.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately and loudly fact-checks Chandler's declaration of love — with total certainty and no context that he knows why Chandler said it.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly timed. Joey's unsolicited correction of Chandler's emotional declaration — with the confidence of someone who knows Chandler's heart — is a great friendship joke. He's not wrong, but his certainty and timing are the joke. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Two hours, that lasted. So did you break up with Joanna?' / 'I think so.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been freed from the handcuffs. Ross asks if he broke up with Joanna.
jokes.punchline: 'I think so' — Chandler's uncertainty about whether a series of traumatic events constitutes a breakup is understated to the point of absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the Chandler-Joanna storyline. 'I think so' is funny because the events were so chaotic that even the status of the relationship is unclear.

jokes.text: Two hours, that lasted. / So did you break up with Joanna? / I think so.
jokes.setup: Chandler returns from the Joanna ordeal. Joey asks if the breakup happened.
jokes.punchline: 'I think so' — Chandler's uncertainty about whether he actually broke up with someone — is the perfect summary of the absurd situation and his usual romantic incompetence.
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler deflation. 'I think so' after all the chaos is a satisfying, understated button on the whole storyline. Character-appropriate and economical.

jokes.text: Ross: 'It's good you got out, before she blew up like Vesuvius.' / 'The volcano?' / 'Speaking of volcanoes, man, are they a violent igneous rock formation!'
jokes.setup: Ross uses 'blew up like Vesuvius' as a metaphor for Joanna's potential anger.
jokes.punchline: Joey literally recognizes the volcano reference, and Ross immediately pivots into an enthusiastic geology lecture — revealing he's been waiting for any opportunity to use his new encyclopedia knowledge.
jokes.explanation: A great callback payoff for the encyclopedia subplot. Joey has apparently been reading his V volume and now hijacks the conversation with his new volcano knowledge — 'are they a violent igneous rock formation!' has the enthusiasm of someone who has just learned their first geological fact. The callback is tight, the character work is excellent, and it sets up the extended volcano sequence.

jokes.text: Chandler's escalating deflection from volcano talk: 'What do you want to talk about? Vivisection? The vas deferens? The Vietnam War?'
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to change the subject from volcanoes. He offers alternatives.
jokes.punchline: All of Chandler's alternatives are other 'V' topics — vivisection, vas deferens, Vietnam War — because Joey only has the V volume of the encyclopedia. Chandler has understood the situation perfectly and is offering topics from Joey's actual knowledge base.
jokes.explanation: Possibly the cleverest structural joke in the episode. Chandler lists V-topics — vivisection, vas deferens, Vietnam War — which is both funny as a random absurd list AND reveals he's figured out that Joey bought the V volume. The joke works on two levels simultaneously: as absurdist wordplay and as a character-insight punchline. This is smart sitcom writing. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: 'Korea's a beautiful country. With such a sad history. Could there be more Kims?'
jokes.setup: Joey has pivoted from volcanoes to talking about the Korean War (staying in the V-to-K range, or following a tangent from the V volume).
jokes.punchline: 'Could there be more Kims?' — Joey's observation about Korean surnames is delivered as a profound anthropological puzzle, and it echoes Chandler's signature 'Could this BE...' construction.
jokes.explanation: 'Could there be more Kims' is a funny observation delivered as a genuine bewilderment. The Chandler-esque phrasing from Joey is a nice touch. Joey's encyclopedic curiosity — 'such a sad history' said with genuine feeling — is sweet and funny.

jokes.text: Joanna's assistant Sophie enters with sesame bagels, sees Chandler handcuffed: '...so I have sesame... Oh, my word!'
jokes.setup: The episode's final Chandler-cuffed scene. Sophie enters expecting a normal office morning.
jokes.punchline: Sophie's discovery — signaled by 'Oh, my word!' — is the episode's closing physical comedy beat. The bagels-to-handcuffs transition is a perfect mundane-to-absurd cut.
jokes.explanation: A solid closing callback to the handcuff plot. 'Oh, my word!' as a reaction to finding someone handcuffed in an office is fittingly understated. The bagels detail grounds it in normalcy before the absurdity hits.

jokes.text: 'I've had a slight office mishap.'
jokes.setup: Sophie has discovered Chandler handcuffed to a chair in his ex-girlfriend's office.
jokes.punchline: 'A slight office mishap' is a masterpiece of understatement for what has been an hours-long bondage situation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'A slight office mishap' is Chandler at peak Chandler — the total composure, the catastrophic understatement, the word 'slight' doing enormous comedic work. This would work as a standalone clip. The economy is near-perfect: five words that summarize the absurdity of everything that's happened while maintaining Chandler's dignity (sort of).

jokes.text: 'Tell your friend Chandler we're definitely broken up now!'
jokes.setup: Sophie has retrieved the key and presumably freed Chandler. Joanna exits.
jokes.punchline: Joanna addresses the message to Sophie to deliver to 'your friend Chandler' — refusing to speak to him directly while he's presumably standing right there — and confirms the breakup in the most withering possible way.
jokes.explanation: A strong closing button. Joanna's refusal to acknowledge Chandler directly — speaking to Sophie as an intermediary while he's present — is a great power move. 'Definitely broken up now' confirms that the series of events has resolved the question from joke #79.

tmdb_overview: Monica caters a party for her mother, who still doesn't quite know how to talk to her daughter. Chandler's encounter with Rachel's boss leads to an embarrassing situation. And an encyclopedia salesman takes advantage of Joey.
insight: 60 jokes in 22 minutes, but weak impact—character work can't sustain mid-tier humor density.
